question: Under Michigan law, every PFD carried to satisfy the carriage requirement must meet which three conditions?
choice_a: It must be brand new, orange in color, and stored in a locked compartment
choice_b: It must be Coast Guard issued, less than one year old, and worn at all times
choice_c: It must be in good and serviceable condition, be the proper size for the intended wearer, and be readily accessible
choice_d: It must be inflatable, size extra-large, and stored below deck
explanation: Every PFD on board must be in good and serviceable condition, be the proper size for the intended wearer, and be readily accessible.
source_note: Overview of PFD Law, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: What does 'readily accessible' mean regarding a PFD under Michigan boating law?
choice_a: The PFD must be worn by every occupant at all times, regardless of conditions
choice_b: The PFD must remain in its original manufacturer packaging until an emergency occurs
choice_c: The PFD must be locked in a dry storage compartment below deck
choice_d: You must be able to put the PFD on in a reasonable amount of time in an emergency, such as a vessel sinking or catching fire
explanation: Readily accessible means you must be able to put the PFD on in a reasonable amount of time in an emergency, such as when a vessel is sinking or on fire.
source_note: Overview of PFD Law, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Unlike the general boating rule that only requires children under 6 to wear a PFD, what rule applies to every person riding on or being towed behind a PWC in Michigan, regardless of age?
choice_a: Every person riding on or being towed behind a PWC must wear a USCG-approved wearable (Type I, II, or III) PFD
choice_b: Only the PWC operator is required to wear a PFD; passengers are exempt
choice_c: PWC riders may substitute a throwable device instead of wearing a PFD
choice_d: PWC riders are exempt from PFD requirements if operating at slow, no-wake speed
explanation: Each person riding on a PWC or being towed behind a PWC or other vessel must wear a USCG-approved Type I, II, or III PFD, regardless of age.
source_note: Specific PFD Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: An approved fire extinguisher intended to satisfy Michigan's carriage requirement must display which marking on its label?
choice_a: 'Automotive Grade' followed by a UL certification number
choice_b: 'Marine Type USCG Approved' followed by the type and size symbols and the approval number
choice_c: 'Residential Use Only' followed by a manufacture date
choice_d: A simple checkmark with no additional text required
explanation: Approved fire extinguishers are identified by the marking 'Marine Type USCG Approved,' followed by the type and size symbols and the approval number.
source_note: Requirements to Carry Fire Extinguishers, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Per the USCG fire extinguisher equipment chart used in Michigan's boater safety course, a vessel 26 feet up to (but less than) 40 feet long WITHOUT a fixed (built-in) extinguishing system must carry what minimum extinguisher(s)?
choice_a: One 5-B extinguisher only
choice_b: Four B-I extinguishers
choice_c: Two B-I extinguishers, or one B-II extinguisher
choice_d: No portable extinguisher is required if the vessel has an open deck
explanation: A vessel 26 feet up to less than 40 feet long without a fixed extinguishing system must carry two B-I extinguishers, or one B-II extinguisher.
source_note: USCG fire extinguisher equipment chart (33 CFR 175.320), as applied in Michigan's boater safety course

question: If a vessel 26 feet up to 40 feet long has a USCG-approved fixed fire-extinguishing system installed in the machinery space, how many portable extinguishers must it still carry?
choice_a: Two B-II extinguishers
choice_b: Three 5-B extinguishers
choice_c: No portable extinguisher is required
choice_d: One B-I extinguisher
explanation: A vessel 26 feet up to 40 feet long with an approved fixed extinguishing system in the machinery space need only carry one B-I portable extinguisher.
source_note: USCG fire extinguisher equipment chart (33 CFR 175.320), as applied in Michigan's boater safety course

question: For a gasoline-powered vessel built in a way that could trap fumes, Michigan's boater safety course requires the vessel to have at least what ventilation ducting?
choice_a: Two ventilation ducts fitted with cowls to remove fumes
choice_b: A single sealed duct with no cowl
choice_c: One duct only, located at the bow
choice_d: No ducts, only an open hatch
explanation: Gasoline-powered vessels constructed in a way that would entrap fumes must have at least two ventilation ducts fitted with cowls to remove the fumes.
source_note: Ventilation System Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: In a natural ventilation system, where must at least one exhaust duct extend?
choice_a: From the engine only up to the flybridge
choice_b: From the open atmosphere down to the lower bilge
choice_c: From the fuel tank directly to the transom
choice_d: It is optional and not regulated
explanation: At least one exhaust duct in a natural ventilation system must extend from the open atmosphere to the lower bilge.
source_note: Ventilation System Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Where must at least one intake duct in a natural ventilation system extend to?
choice_a: The highest point of the cabin roof only
choice_b: Directly into the fuel tank
choice_c: A point at least midway to the bilge or below the level of the carburetor air intake
choice_d: It must terminate above the waterline only, with no depth requirement
explanation: At least one intake duct must extend from a point at least midway to the bilge or below the level of the carburetor air intake.
source_note: Ventilation System Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Before starting the engine of a vessel equipped with a power ventilation system, or after fueling, how long should the blower be run?
choice_a: At least thirty seconds
choice_b: At least one hour
choice_c: Blowers do not need to run before starting the engine
choice_d: At least four minutes
explanation: A power ventilation system's blower should be run for at least four minutes before starting the engine, and after fueling.
source_note: Ventilation System Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: A PWC typically has no power ventilation system. What should the operator do before starting the engine to check for trapped fumes?
choice_a: Open the engine compartment and sniff for gasoline fumes
choice_b: Run the bilge pump for ten minutes
choice_c: Start the engine briefly, then shut it off to test for backfire
choice_d: Spray water into the engine compartment
explanation: For vessels not equipped with a power ventilation system, such as a PWC, the operator should open the engine compartment and sniff for gasoline fumes before starting the engine.
source_note: Ventilation System Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Vessels built after what date, if equipped with power exhaust blowers in gasoline engine compartments, must display a warning sticker near the instrument panel?
choice_a: January 1, 1990
choice_d: January 1, 2000
explanation: Vessels built after July 31, 1980, that contain power exhaust blowers in gasoline engine compartments must have a warning sticker placed near the instrument panel.
source_note: Ventilation System Requirements, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Aside from the specific decibel limits, what basic equipment does Michigan law require a vessel's engine to have for noise reduction?
choice_a: A catalytic converter certified for automotive use
choice_b: No muffler is required as long as the operator wears hearing protection
choice_c: A factory-installed muffler or exhaust system, or another effective muffling system
choice_d: A muffler is required only on vessels used for racing
explanation: A vessel's engine must have a factory-installed muffler or exhaust system for noise reduction, or another effective muffling system.
source_note: Mufflers and Noise Level Limits, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: On state waters, a vessel 26 feet or longer operating under engine power must have a sound-producing device (whistle) audible for at least what distance?
choice_a: One-half mile
choice_b: Two miles
choice_c: One-quarter mile
choice_d: One mile
explanation: A vessel 26 feet or longer under engine power on state waters requires a whistle audible for at least one mile.
source_note: Requirements to Have Sound-Producing Devices, If on State Waters, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: On federally controlled waters (such as the Great Lakes), a vessel 39.4 feet (12 meters) or longer must have a sound signal audible for at least one-half mile and lasting how long?
choice_a: 4 to 6 seconds
choice_b: 10 to 15 seconds
choice_c: Less than 1 second
choice_d: 20 seconds or more
explanation: On federally controlled waters, a vessel 39.4 feet or longer must have a sound signal audible for at least one-half mile, lasting 4 to 6 seconds.
source_note: Requirements to Have Sound-Producing Devices, If on Federally Controlled Waters, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Michigan's boater safety course states that vessels on federally controlled waters, such as the Great Lakes, must be equipped with what?
choice_a: A ship's bell only
choice_b: USCG-approved visual distress signals (VDSs)
choice_c: A radar reflector
choice_d: No additional equipment beyond state-water requirements
explanation: Vessels on federally controlled waters, such as the Great Lakes, must be equipped with USCG-approved visual distress signals.
source_note: Requirements to Carry Visual Distress Signals (VDSs), Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: What are the specifications of the non-pyrotechnic distress flag accepted as a day-only VDS in Michigan?
choice_a: At least 1 by 1 foot, solid red with no markings
choice_b: A white flag with a blue anchor symbol, any size
choice_c: At least 3 by 3 feet, with a black square and ball on an orange background
choice_d: It must be fluorescent green and triangular
explanation: The distress flag is a day signal only and must be at least 3 by 3 feet with a black square and ball on an orange background.
source_note: Non-Pyrotechnic VDSs, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Which pyrotechnic VDS devices are approved for daytime use only?
choice_a: Red flares
choice_b: Red meteors
choice_c: All pyrotechnic VDS devices work equally well day and night
choice_d: Orange smoke signals (handheld and floating)
explanation: Handheld and floating orange smoke signals are pyrotechnic VDSs approved for daytime use only.
source_note: Pyrotechnic VDSs, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Which pyrotechnic VDS devices are approved for both day and night use?
choice_a: Red meteors and red flares
choice_b: Orange smoke signals only
choice_c: Electric distress lights
choice_d: Distress flags
explanation: Red meteors and red flares are pyrotechnic VDSs suitable for both day and night signaling.
source_note: Pyrotechnic VDSs, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: How should pyrotechnic VDS devices be stored aboard a vessel?
choice_a: Submerged in the bilge to prevent overheating
choice_b: In a cool, dry, and prominently marked location
choice_c: Loose in the glove compartment of a tow vehicle
choice_d: Storage location does not matter as long as they are on board
explanation: Pyrotechnic devices should be stored in a cool, dry, and prominently marked location.
source_note: Pyrotechnic VDSs, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Why must pistol-launched and handheld parachute flares or meteors be handled with particular caution?
choice_a: They are illegal for use anywhere in the United States
choice_b: They cannot legally be stored on board any vessel
choice_c: They have many characteristics of a firearm, and some states classify and restrict them as such
choice_d: They require a special boating license endorsement to purchase
explanation: Pistol-launched and handheld parachute flares and meteors have many characteristics of a firearm and must be handled with caution; in some states they are considered a firearm and are prohibited from use.
source_note: Pyrotechnic VDSs, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Besides between sunset and sunrise, when else must a vessel operator display proper navigation lights?
choice_a: Only when another vessel is within 100 yards
choice_b: Only while docked
choice_c: Navigation lights are never required during daylight regardless of visibility
choice_d: During periods of restricted visibility, such as fog or heavy rain
explanation: Navigation lights must be displayed away from the dock between sunset and sunrise, and also during periods of restricted visibility such as fog or heavy rain.
source_note: Overview of Navigation Lights Law, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Who is permitted to use blue or red flashing lights on a vessel in Michigan?
choice_a: Law enforcement vessels only
choice_b: Any vessel operating at night
choice_c: Any vessel towing a PWC
choice_d: Commercial fishing vessels only
explanation: Blue or red flashing lights are restricted to use by law enforcement vessels only.
source_note: Overview of Navigation Lights Law, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: What does Michigan's navigation lights law say about exhibiting other lights on a vessel?
choice_a: Any additional decorative lighting is permitted regardless of color
choice_b: No other lights that may be mistaken for required navigation lights may be exhibited
choice_c: Extra white lights of any number and placement are always permitted
choice_d: There is no restriction on additional lighting of any kind
explanation: No other lights that may be mistaken for required navigation lights may be exhibited on a vessel.
source_note: Overview of Navigation Lights Law, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: Under Michigan law, when must a vessel display an all-round white light while anchored in or connected to the Great Lakes?
choice_a: Only during a declared storm warning
choice_b: Only when anchored more than 1 mile from shore
choice_c: Between sunset and sunrise
choice_d: Anchor lights are never required in Michigan
explanation: All vessels are required to use an all-round white light between sunset and sunrise whenever they are anchored in the waters of or connected to the Great Lakes.
source_note: Required Lights: All Vessels When Not Underway, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: A power-driven vessel less than 26 feet long, when underway at night, may show which lighting configuration instead of separate masthead and sternlights?
choice_a: A single red light at the bow only
choice_b: No white light at all, if sidelights are shown
choice_c: A green light at the stern instead of a masthead light
choice_d: A single all-round white light, in addition to sidelights
explanation: A power-driven vessel less than 26 feet long may show an all-round white light, in addition to sidelights, instead of a separate masthead light and sternlight.
source_note: Required Lights: Power-Driven Vessels When Underway, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: On a power-driven vessel less than 26 feet long, how must the all-round white light (or masthead light) be positioned relative to the sidelights?
choice_a: Higher than the sidelights
choice_b: Lower than the sidelights
choice_c: At exactly the same height as the sidelights
choice_d: Height placement is not regulated for vessels under 26 feet
explanation: On a vessel less than 26 feet long, the all-round white light or masthead light must be higher than the sidelights.
source_note: Required Lights: Power-Driven Vessels When Underway, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: An unpowered vessel less than 26 feet long, when underway at night, must exhibit which lights if practical?
choice_a: No lights are required regardless of conditions
choice_b: The same lights required for unpowered vessels 26 feet or longer
choice_c: Only a single green light at the bow
choice_d: Only a flashing amber light
explanation: If practical, an unpowered vessel less than 26 feet long must exhibit the lights required for unpowered vessels 26 feet or longer.
source_note: Required Lights: Unpowered Vessels Less Than 26 Feet When Underway, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)

question: If it is not practical for an unpowered vessel less than 26 feet long to exhibit the lights required of larger unpowered vessels, what must be kept on hand instead?
choice_a: A pyrotechnic flare, to be set off continuously while underway
choice_b: Nothing; no alternative is provided by law
choice_c: At least one lantern or flashlight shining a white light, ready to display in time to prevent collision
choice_d: A radar reflector
explanation: If it is not practical to exhibit the full navigation lights, the vessel must have on hand at least one lantern or flashlight shining a white light, ready to be displayed in time to prevent a collision.
source_note: Required Lights: Unpowered Vessels Less Than 26 Feet When Underway, Michigan Boater Safety Course (boat-ed.com/michigan)
